Can VoiceOver understand the bookmark?

A custom bookmark icon looks right. Make its action understandable without seeing the screen.

The problem

A custom icon toggles a bookmark and changes from outline to solid. A sighted person can see the difference. What information can a person using VoiceOver get?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

Accessibility semantics are UI descriptions that a device's assistive technology can use, such as a label, a role, a current state or an action. On iOS, the screen reader is VoiceOver. Compose Multiplatform maps its semantics data to native accessibility services.

For this bookmark, expose what the control does and whether the item is currently saved. Prefer a control that already represents a toggle, then give it a meaningful label and expose the checked state. Keep the icon decorative if the surrounding control already provides the complete description.

SituationWhat the user should be able to learn
Focus before savingWhich item the action applies to and whether it is saved
Activate the controlThat bookmarking can be toggled
Focus after savingThat the item is now saved

A visual check proves part of the behavior. On an iPhone, verify focus order, spoken meaning and whether activating the item changes the state. Test a native field embedded in the same screen independently as well. At the hosting boundary, its view and interaction differ from the surrounding shared UI.

Go deeperDesign a two-platform check
What would a useful check record if the same icon works on iOS and Android?

Record the focused control, distinguish its saved and unsaved states, activate it with the platform screen reader, and verify the result. Keep platform-specific wording separate from the intended meaning.

What you now know

Compose semantics describe meaning and actions independently from pixels. On iOS the mapping to native accessibility information makes those semantics available to VoiceOver.
